title: Explore the OSI layers and TCP/IP mapping
note: Conceptual correspondence, not a claim that implementations have seven separate modules. OSI layers 5-7 usually fall within the TCP/IP application grouping; the four-layer model groups physical and link functions together.

parts.name: Layer 7: Application
parts.purpose: Defines the network service and meaning of an exchange for applications. It is the protocol behavior, not simply the entire browser or other user interface.
parts.connect: TCP/IP teaching correspondence: Application. Typical unit: Application data / messages.
parts.advanced: A successful lower-layer connection does not prove a correct application result. Authentication, authorization and business rules can fail even with healthy connectivity.

parts.name: Layer 6: Presentation
parts.purpose: Concerns how information is represented so communicating applications interpret it consistently. Think of encoding, serialization and negotiated representation.
parts.connect: TCP/IP teaching correspondence: Application. Typical unit: Represented application data.
parts.advanced: Do not force every implementation into a separate layer-six module. Encryption is often placed here in teaching diagrams, but real TLS and other security protocols cross model boundaries.

parts.name: Layer 5: Session
parts.purpose: Concerns coordination of a communication dialog, including establishing, managing and ending it and, in some designs, synchronization or recovery points.
parts.connect: TCP/IP teaching correspondence: Application. Typical unit: Dialog / session data.
parts.advanced: An application login session, a TCP connection and an OSI session-layer service are different concepts. One login can span many connections, and one connection can carry many application exchanges.

parts.name: Layer 4: Transport
parts.purpose: Provides transport communication between endpoints. TCP supplies an ordered byte stream; UDP provides datagrams without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees.
parts.connect: TCP/IP teaching correspondence: Transport. Typical unit: TCP segment / UDP datagram.
parts.advanced: TCP flow control concerns receiver capacity; congestion control concerns network conditions. Reliability and encryption are separate properties. QUIC builds secure stream transport over UDP and does not fit a naive one-protocol-per-layer picture.

parts.name: Layer 3: Network
parts.purpose: Addresses and forwards packets across networks. A routing decision selects a next hop rather than delivering a file or authenticating a user.
parts.connect: TCP/IP teaching correspondence: Internet. Typical unit: IP packet / datagram.
parts.advanced: IP does not guarantee ordered or successful delivery. MTU behavior differs between IPv4 and IPv6. NAT, where present, changes addressing and sometimes ports; it is not the same function as routing.

parts.name: Layer 2: Data link
parts.purpose: Carries data across the current link. Ethernet framing includes local-link address information and error detection; other link technologies have their own formats.
parts.connect: TCP/IP teaching correspondence: Link / network access. Typical unit: Frame.
parts.advanced: A routed path normally gets a new link-layer envelope at each hop. Device labels are not exclusive layer assignments: a multilayer switch can also route.

parts.name: Layer 1: Physical
parts.purpose: Transmits encoded signals over a medium: electrical, optical or radio. Connectors, cabling and radio conditions are part of the physical path.
parts.connect: TCP/IP teaching correspondence: Link / network access. Typical unit: Encoded signals / symbols carrying bits.
parts.advanced: Bandwidth, interference, damaged cabling and optical or radio conditions can limit communication. A physical link indicator does not establish IP reachability or application health.

title: Explore a motherboard
note: Generic desktop board, viewed from above. Locations, connectors and supported devices vary by model. This is a teaching illustration, not a picture of your computer.

parts.name: CPU socket
parts.purpose: Holds the processor and connects it electrically to the board. The cooler normally sits above it.
parts.connect: Install only a processor supported by the socket, chipset and firmware.
parts.advanced: A matching physical socket alone does not establish complete CPU support. Consult the exact board compatibility list.

parts.name: DIMM memory slots
parts.purpose: Hold the system RAM used for active programs and data.
parts.connect: Use the supported memory generation and follow the board manual slot order.
parts.advanced: DDR generations are not interchangeable. Channel layout and the recommended two-module slots depend on the board.

parts.name: PCIe expansion slot
parts.purpose: Connects expansion cards such as a graphics card or additional network adapter.
parts.connect: The illustrated long slot is a physical x16-style slot.
parts.advanced: Physical length does not guarantee the number of active electrical lanes; CPU, chipset and other devices can affect lane availability.

parts.name: M.2 storage socket
parts.purpose: Mounts a compact module directly on the board; shown here with an illustrative SSD installed.
parts.connect: Check keying, module length and supported protocol before choosing an SSD.
parts.advanced: M.2 describes a form factor and connector family. A socket may support PCIe/NVMe, SATA, or a documented subset; shape alone does not prove compatibility.

parts.name: SATA data ports
parts.purpose: Carry storage data between the board and compatible SATA drives.
parts.connect: A separate power connection from the power supply is also required for a typical SATA drive.
parts.advanced: SATA data and power connectors are different. Some boards share resources between SATA and M.2 connections.

parts.name: 24-pin main power
parts.purpose: Supplies major motherboard power rails from a compatible power supply.
parts.connect: Connect the designated main ATX motherboard power cable.
parts.advanced: Do not infer power-cable interchangeability from similar appearance; PSU-side modular cable pinouts can differ between models.

parts.name: CPU power connector
parts.purpose: Provides additional power for the CPU voltage-regulation circuitry.
parts.connect: Use the designated CPU/EPS cable as required by the board.
parts.advanced: CPU/EPS and graphics PCIe power connectors have different assignments. Check labels and documentation; never force a fit.

parts.name: Voltage regulators / VRM
parts.purpose: Convert supplied power into voltages needed by the processor.
parts.connect: These components are board circuitry, not a cable port. Heatsinks often cover them.
parts.advanced: Cooling, power delivery and firmware limits can affect sustained operation. A decorative heatsink is not a performance measurement.

parts.name: Chipset / controller hub
parts.purpose: Coordinates a set of peripheral connections and links them to the processor on this conceptual design.
parts.connect: No user cable connects directly to the illustrated chipset package.
parts.advanced: Modern CPUs also connect directly to some memory and PCIe resources. Not all traffic travels through the chipset.

parts.name: RTC battery
parts.purpose: Supports timekeeping and certain retained settings when external power is absent, depending on design.
parts.connect: A coin-cell holder is shown as an example; replacement procedures depend on the board.
parts.advanced: The operating system and user files are not stored in this battery. Removing it is not a general repair for software faults.

parts.name: Fan header
parts.purpose: Provides the specified fan power and control/tachometer connections.
parts.connect: Connect the appropriate CPU or chassis fan header according to its label.
parts.advanced: Headers differ in current limits and control modes. Fan and lighting connectors are not interchangeable.

parts.name: Internal USB header
parts.purpose: Connects compatible case USB ports to the motherboard.
parts.connect: Match the case lead to the specific header type and keyed layout.
parts.advanced: USB 2.0, front USB 3.x and front USB-C headers can have different shapes and capabilities. The pictured header is schematic.

parts.name: Front-panel header
parts.purpose: Connects case controls and indicators such as the power switch and status LEDs.
parts.connect: Follow the board-specific pin diagram and LED polarity.
parts.advanced: The power button is a control signal, not the main power feed. There is no universal pin arrangement to assume.

parts.name: Front audio header
parts.purpose: Connects compatible front-panel headphone and microphone connections.
parts.connect: Use the designated case audio lead and the exact board header instructions.
parts.advanced: Audio, USB and lighting headers have different electrical meanings even when some pins look similar.

title: Recognize the rear-panel ports
note: Enlarged conceptual rear I/O panel. Port presence, colors, counts and supported features vary. These connector drawings are not to scale.

parts.name: USB Type-A
parts.purpose: A rectangular USB connector used by many keyboards, mice and external devices.
parts.connect: Insert the matching plug in its keyed orientation.
parts.advanced: Connector color is not a reliable guarantee of USB speed, power or feature support.

parts.name: USB Type-C
parts.purpose: A reversible connector shape used for a variety of device connections.
parts.connect: Use a cable and device supporting the features required for the task.
parts.advanced: The shape alone does not promise a specific speed, charging power, video output or Thunderbolt support.

parts.name: HDMI video output
parts.purpose: Carries digital display output, often including audio, to a compatible display.
parts.connect: Use the matching display cable and select the corresponding monitor input.
parts.advanced: Motherboard video output generally requires a supported graphics source and configuration. A discrete GPU may require its own display ports.

parts.name: DisplayPort output
parts.purpose: Another digital display connector family; the full-size outline has a distinctive corner.
parts.connect: Use the matching display connection; release a latch if the cable has one.
parts.advanced: Supported resolution, refresh rate and adapters depend on the source, cable and display capabilities.

parts.name: Ethernet network port
parts.purpose: Accepts an Ethernet cable for a wired network link. The common plug is often called RJ45.
parts.connect: Connect to an intended switch or router LAN port.
parts.advanced: Link lights indicate a physical link or activity; they do not prove that IP addressing, DNS or internet access works.

parts.name: Analog audio jacks
parts.purpose: Connect compatible analog speakers, headphones or microphones according to the assigned jack function.
parts.connect: Check the port symbols and audio configuration rather than relying on color alone.
parts.advanced: Audio jacks can be reassigned by some drivers; the actual input/output role must match the connected device.

title: How a program uses CPU, RAM and storage
note: Illustrative loading sequence, not an electrical timing diagram. Click a device or play the tour to follow the roles.

parts.name: SSD / persistent storage
parts.purpose: Stores program files and data across normal shutdown.
parts.connect: The OS reads the required executable and data from storage.
parts.advanced: Storage capacity is different from RAM capacity. A fast SSD does not eliminate all consequences of insufficient working memory.

parts.name: RAM / working memory
parts.purpose: Holds pages used by active programs and the operating system.
parts.connect: Loaded pages become available for instruction and data access.
parts.advanced: The OS can cache files and may swap pages under pressure. Used memory is not automatically wasted memory.

parts.name: CPU / execution
parts.purpose: Executes program instructions and operates on data through its memory hierarchy.
parts.connect: CPU caches reduce repeated access cost for some instruction and data patterns.
parts.advanced: Cache is smaller than main memory and not identical to it. The real execution system is more complex than this three-device illustration.

parts.name: Display / output
parts.purpose: Shows the application result after the operating system and graphics stack prepare it.
parts.connect: A display connection carries the selected graphics output to a monitor.
parts.advanced: Not every program draws a screen; programs can produce files, network messages or terminal output instead.

title: Follow a packet through network devices
note: A conceptual local network with a remote service. Arrows show a selected direction; real communication also needs a return path.

parts.name: Laptop / endpoint
parts.purpose: Runs the client application and originates an IP packet.
parts.connect: For an off-subnet destination, the local next hop is normally a configured gateway.
parts.advanced: The endpoint still needs correct addressing, routing and application settings.

parts.name: Switch / local link
parts.purpose: Forwards local Ethernet frames toward their link-layer destinations.
parts.connect: Connects endpoints and the gateway on the illustrated LAN.
parts.advanced: An ordinary local-link switch does not replace IP routing between different networks.

parts.name: Router / gateway
parts.purpose: Routes an IP packet between connected networks.
parts.connect: Chooses the appropriate next hop according to the routing configuration.
parts.advanced: Firewalling and NAT may be additional functions, but routing is not the same operation as either one.

parts.name: Provider / transit
parts.purpose: Represents the networks carrying traffic toward the remote service.
parts.connect: Multiple routers and administrative networks may be involved.
parts.advanced: The outbound and return routes can differ. A cloud icon does not mean there is only one device or one trusted operator.

parts.name: Service / destination
parts.purpose: Receives traffic at the intended endpoint and processes the application request.
parts.connect: A response must travel back to the client using a valid path.
parts.advanced: Network reachability alone does not prove authentication, authorization or correct application results.

title: Look inside the network envelopes
note: Nested envelopes illustrate encapsulation. Header layouts and sizes vary; this is a conceptual view, not an exact packet decoder.

parts.name: Link frame
parts.purpose: Carries a packet across the current link. Ethernet is one possible link technology.
parts.connect: Contains information for local-link delivery.
parts.advanced: Routers normally build a new link envelope for the next link; the original Ethernet frame does not cross the entire internet.

parts.name: IP packet
parts.purpose: Carries network-layer source and destination information and an encapsulated payload.
parts.connect: Routing decisions use destination and policy information.
parts.advanced: IPv4 and IPv6 formats differ. A routed hop changes forwarding-related fields; NAT can additionally change addresses where configured.

parts.name: Transport data
parts.purpose: TCP segments or UDP datagrams carry application bytes and transport endpoint information.
parts.connect: Ports help identify the relevant transport endpoint.
parts.advanced: TCP provides an ordered byte stream, while UDP provides datagrams; application reliability can also be implemented above UDP.

parts.name: Application content
parts.purpose: Contains the protocol data the application understands.
parts.connect: Examples include a local HTTP request or a DNS message.
parts.advanced: Encryption can make content opaque to an observer. Packet visibility does not automatically provide readable application data.

title: TCP: a normal connection setup
note: Conceptual message sequence. Timing, packet boundaries, retries and optional messages are simplified. The tour highlights one stage at a time and sends no traffic.

parts.name: SYN
parts.purpose: The client proposes a new connection and initial sequence context.
parts.connect: Client to listening server.
parts.advanced: This is the common active-open pattern; other state transitions exist.

parts.name: SYN-ACK
parts.purpose: The server acknowledges the proposal and supplies its own sequence context.
parts.connect: Server to client.
parts.advanced: A reply does not yet establish application-level success.

parts.name: ACK
parts.purpose: The client acknowledges the server sequence context.
parts.connect: Client to server.
parts.advanced: The transport connection can now carry the application byte stream; it is not encrypted by TCP itself.

title: DHCPv4: initial lease acquisition
note: Conceptual message sequence. Timing, packet boundaries, retries and optional messages are simplified. The tour highlights one stage at a time and sends no traffic.

parts.name: DISCOVER
parts.purpose: The client seeks available configuration service.
parts.connect: Initial client discovery; relays are omitted from this picture.
parts.advanced: This illustrates initial acquisition, not every lease renewal.

parts.name: OFFER
parts.purpose: A server proposes lease configuration.
parts.connect: Server to client.
parts.advanced: An offer is not the final lease acknowledgment.

parts.name: REQUEST
parts.purpose: The client requests the selected configuration.
parts.connect: Client to server.
parts.advanced: Actual addressing and delivery details depend on client state.

parts.name: ACKNOWLEDGE
parts.purpose: The server confirms the configuration.
parts.connect: Server to client.
parts.advanced: The lease has a lifetime; later renewal follows its state rules.

title: DNS: cache miss and resolver work
note: Conceptual message sequence. Timing, packet boundaries, retries and optional messages are simplified. The tour highlights one stage at a time and sends no traffic.

parts.name: Record query
parts.purpose: The client asks for a record for a fictional name.
parts.connect: For example: an address record for example.com.
parts.advanced: The client need not perform the full resolution process itself.

parts.name: Resolve or use cache
parts.purpose: The resolver consults its cache or upstream authorities.
parts.connect: Upstream exchanges are intentionally not drawn.
parts.advanced: A cache hit can omit upstream network exchanges.

parts.name: Answer or error
parts.purpose: The resolver sends a result and response status.
parts.connect: Client inspects record data and applicable lifetime.
parts.advanced: An empty record set, nonexistent name and server failure differ.

parts.name: Application continues
parts.purpose: The client can use the resolved result for a later operation.
parts.connect: A separate application connection follows if needed.
parts.advanced: DNS success does not establish service reachability.

title: TLS 1.3: simplified full-handshake flights
note: Conceptual message sequence. Timing, packet boundaries, retries and optional messages are simplified. The tour highlights one stage at a time and sends no traffic.

parts.name: ClientHello
parts.purpose: The client offers handshake parameters and key-establishment information.
parts.connect: Client begins negotiation.
parts.advanced: Resumption and early data are not shown.

parts.name: Server flight
parts.purpose: The server selects parameters and sends its authenticated handshake flight.
parts.connect: A typical certificate-authenticated flow is illustrated.
parts.advanced: The client must validate the expected peer and handshake.

parts.name: Client Finished
parts.purpose: The client completes its handshake confirmation.
parts.connect: Client to server.
parts.advanced: Optional client-certificate authentication is omitted.

parts.name: Protected application data
parts.purpose: Application data uses the negotiated protection.
parts.connect: Traffic can flow in both directions.
parts.advanced: TLS does not decide application object permissions.

title: Follow encapsulation and decapsulation
note: A simplified endpoint journey for a plaintext HTTP-over-TCP example. The diagram shows conceptual envelopes, not fixed packet sizes or an exact wire trace.

parts.name: Application message
parts.purpose: An application creates a message; this example uses plaintext HTTP over TCP to make the envelopes easy to see.
parts.connect: Sender begins with application bytes.
parts.advanced: HTTPS adds TLS protection and HTTP/3 uses QUIC; neither is drawn as this exact example.

parts.name: Transport encapsulation
parts.purpose: TCP carries the application bytes in its stream and sends segments with transport information.
parts.connect: Conceptual envelope: TCP header plus application bytes.
parts.advanced: One message may span multiple segments; this simplified picture is not a guarantee of one packet per request.

parts.name: IP encapsulation
parts.purpose: IP carries transport data with network-layer address and forwarding information.
parts.connect: Conceptual envelope: IP header around transport data.
parts.advanced: Packet sizing, options and fragmentation behavior depend on protocol and path.

parts.name: Link framing
parts.purpose: The current link carries the IP packet inside a frame suitable for the next hop.
parts.connect: Conceptual envelope: Ethernet header, payload and frame check sequence.
parts.advanced: At a router, a new link frame normally replaces the previous one.

parts.name: Physical transmission
parts.purpose: The link hardware encodes data as signals on the medium.
parts.connect: Signals traverse the cable, fiber or radio link.
parts.advanced: Signals are not another application header. Real encoding and timing depend on the medium.

parts.name: Receiver decapsulation
parts.purpose: The destination processes the link, IP and transport information and delivers reconstructed data to the application.
parts.connect: The receiver conceptually works back up the stack.
parts.advanced: Checks, buffering and reassembly occur where needed; applications must still interpret their own messages.

title: IoT: follow the trust boundaries
note: Select a stage or play the guided tour. Arrows show conceptual flow, not proof of trust.

parts.name: Device
parts.purpose: Reads a sensor or drives an actuator.
parts.connect: Authenticates using its individual identity.
parts.advanced: Keep physical safety constraints independent of network commands.

parts.name: Gateway / broker
parts.purpose: Relays messages or routes publications.
parts.connect: Checks topic permissions for each authenticated client.
parts.advanced: A permitted connection does not grant every topic.

parts.name: Cloud service
parts.purpose: Stores readings and applies policy.
parts.connect: Maps devices to owners and tenants.
parts.advanced: Enforce authorization for every object and operation.

parts.name: User application
parts.purpose: Displays state and requests actions.
parts.connect: Uses a user session to call the service.
parts.advanced: Never trust an owner identifier supplied by the client.

title: IoT: a verified update journey
note: Select a stage or play the guided tour. Arrows show conceptual flow, not proof of trust.

parts.name: Obtain package
parts.purpose: Receives an update and signed metadata.
parts.connect: Treats downloaded bytes as untrusted.
parts.advanced: HTTPS alone does not replace device-side update verification.

parts.name: Verify identity
parts.purpose: Checks signature and payload binding.
parts.connect: Uses an installed trusted signing key.
parts.advanced: A plain checksum does not authenticate a publisher.

parts.name: Check policy
parts.purpose: Checks model, version and eligibility.
parts.connect: Rejects incompatible or unauthorized rollback.
parts.advanced: Plan authenticated recovery and signing-key rotation.

parts.name: Install / recover
parts.purpose: Commits a verified image safely.
parts.connect: Checks health and records the result.
parts.advanced: Interrupted power must not leave the device without a recovery path.

title: Network topology atlas: seven connection patterns
note: Select a layout to compare traffic paths and failure dependencies. Mesh shows a full mesh of four nodes. These are physical connection sketches; forwarding protocols are not simulated.

parts.name: Point-to-point topology
parts.purpose: A single link connects two endpoints. It is easy to understand and troubleshoot.
parts.connect: A routed connection between two routers is a common example. Distinguish a physical cable from a logical tunnel crossing several links.
parts.advanced: One link has no alternate path on its own. Two parallel links may still share a cable duct, power supply or provider.

parts.name: Bus topology
parts.purpose: Devices attach to one shared backbone. Classic coaxial Ethernet is a historical example.
parts.connect: Attached stations share the medium. Cable termination and shared-medium access behavior matter in the relevant technology.
parts.advanced: A backbone fault can affect many stations; outcome depends on the physical implementation. Modern switched Ethernet should not be described as a shared coaxial bus.

parts.name: Star topology
parts.purpose: Each endpoint connects to a central device, often an Ethernet switch or wireless access point.
parts.connect: Failure of one endpoint cable typically isolates that endpoint. Failure of the central device can disconnect all attached endpoints.
parts.advanced: A central hub and a switch can have the same physical star shape but different forwarding behavior. A switch does not inherently provide redundant power or paths.

parts.name: Ring topology
parts.purpose: Each node has two neighbors in a closed loop. The physical ring does not define its forwarding protocol.
parts.connect: Some ring technologies use token passing or protection mechanisms; ordinary Ethernet links arranged in a ring do not automatically provide either.
parts.advanced: Redundant Layer 2 paths need loop prevention or a suitable protection design. An uncontrolled forwarding loop can circulate frames and disrupt the network.

parts.name: Full and partial mesh
parts.purpose: In a full mesh, every node connects directly to every other node. A partial mesh connects only selected pairs.
parts.connect: A full mesh of n nodes needs n(n-1)/2 undirected point-to-point links. Five nodes need ten links; each node has four neighbors.
parts.advanced: Extra paths increase redundancy and operational complexity. Routing or bridging rules must choose usable paths; connectivity alone is not a security policy.

parts.name: Tree and hierarchical topology
parts.purpose: A tree branches from a root through intermediate nodes to leaves. A simple tree has no cycles.
parts.connect: Access switches can connect endpoints to distribution devices. An upstream failure affects the subtree that depends on it.
parts.advanced: Real campus designs often add redundant uplinks and are no longer strict graph-theory trees. Document the actual active paths and failure domains.

parts.name: Spine-leaf topology
parts.purpose: A common data-center design connects each leaf switch to every spine switch. Endpoints attach to leaves.
parts.connect: In a typical routed fabric, traffic between leaves crosses a spine. Equal-cost multipath can distribute flows across available paths.
parts.advanced: Capacity depends on link speeds, counts and traffic patterns. Aggregate offered traffic exceeding uplink capacity creates oversubscription; equal path counts do not imply equal bandwidth.

title: Session lifecycle: where trust changes
note: Select a stage or play the guided tour. This illustration contains no real tokens and performs no network requests.

parts.name: Anonymous
parts.purpose: The browser begins without an authenticated identity.
parts.connect: A temporary identifier may support a shopping cart or preferences.
parts.advanced: Never infer authenticated access from possession of an anonymous identifier.

parts.name: Login / rotate
parts.purpose: The server verifies the login and issues the authenticated session.
parts.connect: Replace the pre-login identifier and remove its authenticated usefulness.
parts.advanced: Rotation must preserve appropriate user state without preserving an attacker-known authenticated credential.

parts.name: Validate requests
parts.purpose: The service checks validity and authorization on each protected operation.
parts.connect: Associate the request with the correct identity and current permissions.
parts.advanced: A valid session is not permission to read every object or act for another user.

parts.name: Logout / expire
parts.purpose: The session loses validity under the application policy.
parts.connect: Enforce invalidation at the service, not only by deleting browser state.
parts.advanced: Retest old credentials and document any deliberate distributed or token-expiry window.

title: Web assessment: six stages from rule to retest
note: Select a stage or play the guided tour. Follow this cycle for each feature; the diagrams do not send requests.

parts.name: Define the rule
parts.purpose: State the security property and permitted actors.
parts.connect: Map an input to its trust boundary and sensitive operation.
parts.advanced: A tool name is not a test hypothesis.

parts.name: Prepare controls
parts.purpose: Create a known-good request and a denied-case expectation.
parts.connect: Use synthetic accounts, objects and a reset method.
parts.advanced: Keep authentication state and other variables consistent.

parts.name: Change one input
parts.purpose: Modify one ownership, state or input condition.
parts.connect: Compare the changed request against the baseline.
parts.advanced: Use bounded local tests and stop on unexpected effects.

parts.name: Verify evidence
parts.purpose: Inspect identity, content and server-side effects.
parts.connect: Eliminate redirects, caches and stale sessions as explanations.
parts.advanced: Status, length or timing alone is rarely sufficient.

parts.name: Repair the cause
parts.purpose: Enforce the rule at the trusted server boundary.
parts.connect: Use appropriate authorization, parsing or transaction controls.
parts.advanced: Suppressing a scanner finding does not repair the root cause.

parts.name: Retest both paths
parts.purpose: Repeat the denied case and a legitimate operation.
parts.connect: Preserve useful assertions as regression tests.
parts.advanced: State untested variants and limits instead of claiming complete coverage.

title: Network testing: four boundaries behind one connection
note: Select a boundary or play the tour. This conceptual path explains what each observation can establish; it does not probe any network.

parts.name: Source zone
parts.purpose: Defines where the observation originates.
parts.connect: Record interface, route and expected permissions.
parts.advanced: A result from one source does not establish every zone policy.

parts.name: Network policy
parts.purpose: Controls permitted traffic between zones.
parts.connect: Correlate probes with applicable firewall evidence.
parts.advanced: A timeout by itself is not a verified policy block.

parts.name: Service listener
parts.purpose: Accepts the transport connection on a bound address and port.
parts.connect: Confirm the service is actually running for the policy test.
parts.advanced: A closed listener does not prove that a firewall would block an active service.

parts.name: Application policy
parts.purpose: Controls identity and allowed operations after transport connection.
parts.connect: Test a legitimate and unauthorized action with synthetic accounts.
parts.advanced: Transport reachability is not permission to access every resource.

title: Forensics: preserve the link from source to conclusion
note: Select a stage or play the tour. This lesson uses synthetic examples and does not collect evidence from your device.

parts.name: Document source
parts.purpose: Identify the item and investigative question.
parts.connect: Record acquisition context, time and handling.
parts.advanced: Source identity is not established by a hash alone.

parts.name: Preserve baseline
parts.purpose: Protect the acquisition and record integrity values.
parts.connect: Create separately identified working copies.
parts.advanced: Live acquisition can change the source; document those effects.

parts.name: Analyze copies
parts.purpose: Extract relevant artifacts into a separate analysis area.
parts.connect: Record tool versions, commands and parser assumptions.
parts.advanced: A parser result needs validation and context.

parts.name: Correlate / report
parts.purpose: Compare independent artifacts and explain uncertainty.
parts.connect: Preserve original timestamps and cite source locations.
parts.advanced: Correlation alone does not prove attribution or causation.

title: Remote access: identity, gateway, target and lifecycle
note: Select a stage or play the guided tour. This conceptual diagram does not open a connection.

parts.name: Client identity
parts.purpose: Uses a named user and protected credentials.
parts.connect: Verifies the expected server or gateway identity.
parts.advanced: Do not treat encryption alone as identity verification.

parts.name: Access gateway
parts.purpose: Provides an approved entry path.
parts.connect: Authenticates access and restricts permitted targets.
parts.advanced: A gateway or VPN is not blanket authorization for the network.

parts.name: Target service
parts.purpose: Accepts the selected SSH, RDP or application session.
parts.connect: Enforces account and resource permissions.
parts.advanced: Reachability and successful login do not imply administrator rights.

parts.name: Audit / revoke
parts.purpose: Records permitted use and ends access when needed.
parts.connect: Revoke credentials and active sessions according to policy.
parts.advanced: Blocking future logins may leave existing sessions active.

title: Network attack analysis: prove each transition
note: Select a stage or play the tour. The model distinguishes a possible path from observed success.

parts.name: Attacker position
parts.purpose: Defines the actual starting access and controllable inputs.
parts.connect: Local-link access, credentials and remote reachability imply different opportunities.
parts.advanced: Do not assume a capability that has not been established.

parts.name: Trust decision
parts.purpose: A receiver chooses whether to accept an identity, message or route.
parts.connect: Identify the exact rule an attacker attempts to influence.
parts.advanced: An input being sent does not prove that it was accepted.

parts.name: Accepted effect
parts.purpose: The receiver changes a mapping, connection, identity or action.
parts.connect: Correlate the resulting behavior with the preceding input.
parts.advanced: Redirection or authentication is not automatically full compromise.

parts.name: Confirmed impact
parts.purpose: The observed operation violates the intended security property.
parts.connect: Preserve evidence and test the control that breaks the path.
parts.advanced: Separate attempts, effects, business impact and untested inferences.
